To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Bone marrow responds to early breast cancer by transcriptional reprogramming of hematopoietic and stromal compartments and by expansion of myelopoiesis.

bone marrow responds to stress signaling from the primary tumor by reprogramming its hematopoietic and stromal compartments and that these early changes can be detected in the peripheral blood through deregulation of microRNAs.

the bone marrow responds to stress induced by the presence of a growing mammary tumor by expanding myelopoietic cells endowed with immunomodulatory properties, and this occurs as early as preinvasive stages of mammary carcinogensis.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of the earliest changes in the bone marrow in association with breast cancer initiation, and with the characterization of circulating microRNas that may represent early markers of bone marrow adaptation.
the study of molecular mechanisms underlying the interaction between tumor cells and bone marrow in the context of early breast cancer.
the early events occurring in the bone marrow during breast cancer development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the bone marrow is an early target of cancer and that the transcriptional changes and deregulation of circulating miRNAs may be exploited as novel diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers.
bone marrow is a site of adaptation to cancer initiation through a process that starts at pre-invasive stage and that can be tracked through deregulation of circulating miRNAs.

bone marrow responds to stress signaling from a growing tumor through transcriptional rewinding toward innate and inflammation programs, which are associated with the expansion of myeolid cells at the expense of B lymphoid cells and deregulated circulating miRNAs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
early bone marrow adaptation is associated with deregulation of miRNAs in circulation and that the bone marrow may sense peripheral cancer initiation.
the bone marrow is able to adapt to the early presence of a tumor through transcriptional reprogramming and stromal changes that are reflected by deregulation of microRNAs in peripheral blood.
the bone marrow is able to sense the presence of a growing mammary carcinoma and responds by reprogramming hematopoiesis and the bone marrow microenvironment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
bone marrow responds to stress induced by a distant cancer by reprogramming the hematopoietics compartment toward a pro-tumorigenic phenotype.

the bone marrow is an active player in the crosstalk between the primary tumor and the systemic environment and that it is possible to detect early bone marrow modifications in association with deregulation of blood microRNA levels.

the bone marrow is an early responder to the stress signals induced by a growing tumor, which may contribute to tumor progression through the expansion of immunosuppressive cells and the re-localization of stromal cells.
